topic: Polymer Chemistry II — natural rubber, Teflon, biodegradable polymers, vulcanisation
description: Advanced polymer topics: natural rubber (polyisoprene, vulcanisation, Goodyear), Buna-S, Teflon (PTFE), biodegradable polymers (PHBV, PLA), neoprene, bakelite formation — complementing CHEM_POLYMERS_MIXED.

questions.stem: Natural rubber is a polymer of which monomer?

options.option_text: Isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene) — natural rubber = cis-polyisoprene
Ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) — this is the monomer of polyethylene, not natural rubber
Styrene (C₆H₅-CH=CH₂) — this is the monomer of polystyrene, not natural rubber
Propylene (CH₃-CH=CH₂) — this is the monomer of polypropylene, not natural rubber

questions.explanation: NATURAL RUBBER = cis-1,4-polyisoprene. Monomer: ISOPRENE = CH₂=C(CH₃)-CH=CH₂ (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene). SOURCE: latex from Hevea brasiliensis tree (Para rubber tree; native to Amazon, now grown in Kerala, India; Thailand = world's top producer). cis CONFIGURATION: natural rubber (elastic, flexible). trans CONFIGURATION = GUTTA-PERCHA (hard, non-elastic — used in golf balls, dental material). GUTTAPERCHA vs RUBBER: same monomer (isoprene), different geometry (trans vs cis). BUTADIENE RUBBER (Buna): polymer of butadiene (CH₂=CH-CH=CH₂) — no methyl group, different from isoprene. SYNTHETIC ISOPRENE RUBBER: can replicate natural rubber — used when supply of natural rubber is scarce. PYQ FREQUENCY: natural rubber monomer in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Chemistry GA, RRB NTPC 1-2× per cycle. MEMORY: 'iSOprene → i for iSOlated-C rubber; ISO = same = cis (same side).'

questions.stem: Vulcanisation of rubber, a process credited to Charles Goodyear (1839), involves treating rubber with:

options.option_text: Sulphur — cross-links the polyisoprene chains, making rubber harder and more elastic
Chlorine — used in neoprene synthesis from chloroprene, not in vulcanisation
Nitrogen — an inert gas used in tyre inflation (nitrogen tyres), not for vulcanisation
Carbon dioxide — used in carbonation or fire suppression, not in rubber processing

questions.explanation: VULCANISATION: heating natural rubber with SULPHUR (S) forms S-S CROSS-LINKS (disulfide bridges) between polyisoprene chains. EFFECT: (1) Increases TENSILE STRENGTH and HARDNESS. (2) Makes rubber ELASTIC over a wider temperature range. (3) Reduces TACKINESS (stickiness) and increases DURABILITY. (4) Prevents CREEP (permanent deformation). CHARLES GOODYEAR: accidentally discovered vulcanisation in 1839 when a rubber-sulphur mixture fell on a hot stove. Goodyear Tires named in his honour. EBONITE (HARD RUBBER): rubber vulcanised with 30-40% sulphur → extremely hard material (used in bowling balls, hockey pucks). Normal tyre rubber: ~1-3% sulphur. INDIA ANGLE: Kerala produces ~90% of India's natural rubber. Rubber Board of India (Kottayam) regulates the sector. PYQ FREQUENCY: vulcanisation + sulphur in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Chemistry, RRB NTPC 1-2× per cycle. MEMORY: VULCAN (Roman god of fire) + sulphur crosslinks = fire + brimstone = tougher rubber.

questions.stem: Teflon (PTFE — polytetrafluoroethylene) is valued in cookware and industrial applications primarily for its:

options.option_text: Non-stick property and extreme chemical inertness due to strong C-F bonds
High electrical conductivity, making it ideal for wiring and electronic circuits
High biodegradability, allowing environmentally safe disposal after use
High transparency to light, making it suitable for optical lenses and windows

questions.explanation: TEFLON (PTFE): polymer of tetrafluoroethylene (CF₂=CF₂). STRUCTURE: carbon backbone fully surrounded by fluorine atoms. C-F bond: very strong (485 kJ/mol) and highly non-polar → nothing sticks to it. PROPERTIES: (1) NON-STICK: food, chemicals — almost nothing adheres. (2) CHEMICALLY INERT: resistant to virtually all acids, bases, solvents. (3) HIGH MELTING POINT: ~327°C (among the highest for a thermoplastic). (4) EXCELLENT ELECTRICAL INSULATOR (not conductor — Option B wrong). (5) LOW FRICTION COEFFICIENT: one of the slipperiest known solids. APPLICATIONS: non-stick cookware, plumber's tape (PTFE tape for pipe sealing), lab equipment, aerospace seals, bearings. DISCOVERY: Roy Plunkett (DuPont), accidentally in 1938. PFOA CONTROVERSY: earlier Teflon manufacturing used PFOA (carcinogenic) — phased out by 2013; modern Teflon is PFOA-free. PYQ FREQUENCY: Teflon properties in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Chemistry GA 1-2× per cycle. MEMORY: 'TEFLON = Tough, Extremely Fluorinated, Low-friction ON cookware.'

questions.stem: Buna-S is a synthetic rubber widely used in tyre manufacturing. It is a copolymer of:

options.option_text: Butadiene and styrene — SBR (styrene-butadiene rubber) known as Buna-S
Butadiene and acrylonitrile — this combination gives Buna-N, used in oil-resistant parts
Isoprene and chloroprene — isoprene gives natural rubber; chloroprene gives neoprene
Styrene and acrylonitrile — SAN copolymer is a thermoplastic, not a rubber elastomer

questions.explanation: BUNA-S = SBR = STYRENE-BUTADIENE RUBBER. Comonomers: butadiene (CH₂=CH-CH=CH₂) + styrene (C₆H₅-CH=CH₂). BUNA comes from: BU = butadiene; NA = natrium (sodium catalyst used in polymerisation). S = styrene. WORLD'S MOST PRODUCED SYNTHETIC RUBBER: ~70% of all synthetic rubber globally. Used in car tyres, shoe soles, conveyor belts. COMPARISON TABLE: BUNA-S = butadiene + styrene (tyre rubber). BUNA-N (Nitrile rubber) = butadiene + acrylonitrile (oil-resistant seals, gloves). NEOPRENE = polychloroprene (from chloroprene CH₂=CCl-CH=CH₂) — weather/oil resistant (wetsuits, gaskets). NATURAL RUBBER = cis-polyisoprene. ADVANTAGES OF BUNA-S OVER NATURAL RUBBER: better abrasion resistance, cheaper, weather resistant. DISADVANTAGE: lower resilience (less bouncy) than natural rubber — natural rubber still preferred in aircraft tyres. PYQ FREQUENCY: Buna-S composition in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Chemistry 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Bakelite, the first truly synthetic polymer, is formed by the condensation polymerisation of:

options.option_text: Phenol and formaldehyde — they condense with loss of water to form a cross-linked network
Urea and formaldehyde — this forms urea-formaldehyde resin (used in adhesives), not bakelite
Melamine and formaldehyde — this forms melamine resin (crockery), not bakelite
Aniline and phthalic anhydride — this forms an alkyd resin (paint), not bakelite

questions.explanation: BAKELITE = PHENOL-FORMALDEHYDE (PF) resin. INVENTOR: Leo Baekeland (Belgian-American), 1907. First fully synthetic polymer (not derived from natural sources). REACTION: phenol (C₆H₅OH) + formaldehyde (HCHO) → condensation (loss of H₂O) → cross-linked 3D network polymer (thermoset). THERMOSETTING: once set, cannot be remelted — cross-linked structure is permanent. PROPERTIES: excellent electrical insulator, heat-resistant, hard, brittle. APPLICATIONS: electrical switches, sockets, handles of cookers, billiard balls (historically). COMPARISON: (1) UREA-FORMALDEHYDE RESIN: electrical fittings (white-coloured), wood adhesives. (2) MELAMINE-FORMALDEHYDE: hard plastic crockery, table surfaces (Formica). (3) BAKELITE: electrical applications (dark brown). EPOXY RESIN: bisphenol-A + epichlorohydrin — adhesives. PYQ FREQUENCY: bakelite composition in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC Chemistry 1-2× per cycle. MEMORY: 'BAKE-lite = BAKE it hard (thermosetting) from Phenol + aldehyde.'

questions.stem: PHBV (polyhydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate) is significant in environmental chemistry because it is:

options.option_text: A biodegradable polymer produced by bacterial fermentation, breaking down in soil and water
A synthetic condensation polymer with high UV resistance used in greenhouse coverings
A conducting polymer used in solar cells and organic LED displays in electronics
A thermosetting resin used in aircraft composites for its extremely high heat resistance

questions.explanation: PHBV (polyhydroxybutyrate-co-hydroxyvalerate): a naturally occurring BIODEGRADABLE POLYESTER produced by bacteria (Ralstonia eutropha and others) as an intracellular carbon/energy storage material. BIODEGRADATION: microbes in soil and water degrade PHBV completely into CO₂ and H₂O (aerobic) or CH₄ and CO₂ (anaerobic) within months. ADVANTAGES OVER CONVENTIONAL PLASTICS: (1) biodegrades without toxic residues. (2) biocompatible (used in surgical sutures, drug delivery). (3) produced from renewable feedstocks (sugars, CO₂). APPLICATIONS: packaging, medical implants, drug-delivery capsules, agricultural films. OTHER BIODEGRADABLE POLYMERS: PLA (polylactic acid — from corn/sugarcane fermentation; used in 3D printing filaments, food packaging); PCL (polycaprolactone — medical sutures). CHALLENGE: PHBV is more expensive than conventional plastics — main barrier to widespread adoption. UPSC ANGLE: plastic pollution, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) policies, India's single-use plastic ban 2022. PYQ FREQUENCY: biodegradable polymers in UPSC Prelims GS-3, SSC CGL Chemistry GA, IBPS PO — 1× per 2-3 years.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes addition polymerisation from condensation polymerisation?

options.option_text: Addition: monomers join without losing any atoms; product is the only output. Condensation: monomers release a small molecule (H₂O, HCl, NH₃) as a by-product
Addition: always forms branched-chain polymers. Condensation: always forms linear, unbranched chains too
Addition: only natural polymers like rubber and starch form via this route. Condensation: only synthetic fibres like nylon use this mechanism
Addition: requires high pressure and metal catalysts only. Condensation: occurs only at room temperature without any catalyst

questions.explanation: ADDITION POLYMERISATION: unsaturated monomers (alkenes) join by opening double bonds → polymer molecular formula = n × (monomer formula). NO BY-PRODUCT. Examples: Polyethylene (-CH₂-CH₂-)_n from ethylene; PVC from vinyl chloride; Polystyrene from styrene; Teflon from tetrafluoroethylene. CONDENSATION POLYMERISATION: bifunctional monomers react and LOSE a small molecule at each bond formation. By-products: H₂O (polyesters, nylons), HCl (some silicones). Examples: Nylon-6,6 from hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid (H₂O lost); Dacron/Terylene from ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid (H₂O lost); Bakelite from phenol + formaldehyde (H₂O lost). OPTION B is wrong — branching depends on polymerisation conditions (LDPE is branched; HDPE is linear; both are addition polymers). OPTION C is wrong — starch and cellulose are actually condensation polymers of glucose! Addition polymers include synthetic materials. UPSC NICHE: Cellulose = condensation polymer (n glucose units − (n-1) H₂O molecules); examiner favourite trap. PYQ FREQUENCY: addition vs condensation in SSC CGL Tier-2 Chemistry, IBPS PO, UPSC CSAT 1-2× per year.
